text:
The clock is ticking like a woodpecker burring a hole in my skull. Four hours left to go and I am nowhere near the space in time I want to reside in. Two years a waste of nothing but a good bourbon on my shelf, leaving me with scars I never thought possible.

We are in this together, aging. 10, 20, 30… Going on 60 soon enough to be caught under a wave of past experiences that should have happened, yet never did. Regret, an enemy of the soul, leaving it empty just enough you want to fill it with your future. The present never seems to fit into this equation.

It all fades eventually though. The sun does rise, the moments do come, and those blip few seconds where your eyelashes collide in a blink, make you just another moment wiser.

A shared timeline of breaths taken makes us human, so I say let's continue breathing till death do us part.

I glow in the dark when the world that's wrapped around me suffocates me into oblivion once or twice. Closed eyelids don't help the odd oozy liquid escaping the corners of my eyes. I wish it was a different feeling, maybe a little less sharp when I breathe in, but the stabbing pain persists into nightfall when the shadows are already asleep. A sudden feel of failure enwraps my rays bouncing off the walls of the room; my life a night club with VIP attendance.

A troubling feeling I am familiar with, almost like a friend that comes to visit just to make sure I'm not ok and can lend a superficial helping hand.

I glow in the dark when the screaming isn't loud enough to pierce my dogs ears who sleeps soundly through the jackhammers in my head. My vocal cords wounded from the alcohol hitting everything but my bloodstream, slowly killing my familiar insanity. I hear nothing but thumping that self regulates at an irregular speed inside my chest. My rosy complexion turns snow white and nothing but my seven bottles of wine dig in my mind when home from work I go.

I glow in the dark when the sun finally comes out but I am still stuck in the closet. These clothes aren't mine, my brain slipping into a dream-like cocktail of bourgeois puppets being pulled in all directions by a master who can't make up their mind. A theatrical failure on an empty stage with a full audience to judge an undeveloped form of art.

It's just that time of the month.

They call me boring most days.

They might be right. I don't like getting out the house much. Forced chains around my neck pulling me toward hells basement, I paint the perfect picket fence picturesque house wife. My skirt just short enough to be fun, long enough to be appropriate, and colored all sorts of cupcake fun. I wear heels, not too high, not to thin, boring colored, toes bubble gum pink. Hair pulled back, but not too tight, that would be too confident.

Husband's out most days, the kids a load I carry with a smile. Love the little mistakes I've made running around my kitchen.

Then night falls. House cleaned, husbands lover keeping him busy, kids snoring like chainsaws, and the lights dimmed to the perfect magazine shade of poise.

My heels come off, skirt neatly folded on the dryer, my underwear color matched with the bottle of red I keep in the fridge. I like mine cold and poisonous.

Music's on, TV's off. Im dancing in a glittered sprinkled slimy dreamlike state all the way to the pool. I jump in.

"Wake up!"

Hungover. Single. Naked.

Welcome to the good life.

I fell asleep. Again. All I remember is yelling and the couch in my face. Rough night.

He isn't here. I wonder why. Maybe he needed space. Or maybe he isn't coming back.

My dog is hungry. His bowl is filled with a bottle of rum I spilled. He doesn't seem to want it. Allow me then.

Where are my cigarettes? The only things I ever constantly lose and always need. Fuck.

Who's she? Hello? I guess she stayed the night. I don't speak German. Excuse me.

The kitchen's a mess. I'm ignoring it. Need coffee. Stepping over leftover food on the floor. Swell.

Stepped on broken glass. The pain is nice. Good morning, sun-shiny day. Where did I put down that dog bowl?

He's back. Kissed me. Kissed her. She definitely slept here last night. Good.

Who is he? I don't know you. She at least feels familiar. Coffee tastes good right now. Lighter please.

I'm not wearing underwear. My bra is too tight. This is uncomfortable.

Sure, you can have one. I should light it for her too. She speaks my language. I like her lips.

The silence is awkward. Should I say something to break this stance of shame?

She kissed me. Hm. I'll kiss her back. She feels known. I've been here before. He's back. I'm home.

Let me tell you a story about Mr. Eeky-Weeky and his uncanny ability to make things out of fuzz.

He was a small thing, that Mr. Eeky-Weeky, yet charming as can be. A little push is all it took for Mr. Eeky-Weeky to rise above his humdrum job to his multi-billion business named Fuzz It All.

Let's go back a little though, to a place where he once needed. A place real small, where he was born, not that tall, but he called it home.

"Fresh baked cookies and a coffee pot, the smell of fresh croissants. Not quite a breakfast of champions, but close enough", he thought.

On one sunny day, as breakfast came and went, he thought "I think the day's too clear!" He jumped up high, with a half impressed smile, then sat back down to think. "I think, I think" but nothing came. He thought again, "I think, I think," and still the same. His brain a door that wouldn't open, even for the best of his mindful voices.

Another day would come and go until 100 days later, he finally spoke:

"A day too clear needs a fuzzy reinvention, an unconventional decor. It needs the sound of fuzz to ring soundtracks at passersbys, playing music at romantic restaurants. It needs curly dresses that twirl beneath the seams at the hips, fuzzy love on the skins of those who wear it.

It needs an oil painting across the river created by a master, capturing the fuzzy houses in the reflection of the water as the photos taken of the passing cars capture forever the insanity of speed with a fuzz-like exposure."

A fuzzy idea. Not very polished, but enough, he thought, to make a leash for puppy Olie he loved too much for words to... "Ah, I lost it."

He leaned down to find the wind was blowing from underneath the table he was hard at working. And there he saw it, a pile of fuzz from little Olie, whose time for shedding was prime in its glory.

And there it started and there it went. A leash, a collar, and soon a dress, for fuzz had no limits to address. He worked and worked on laces, and hats, and on many things until, at last, he tailored a beautiful coat that made its way to runways, fashionistas, and headlines. Mr. Eeky-Weeky became a sensation overnight, and he soon became the fashion icon of Milan; the world cheered at all his creations, and only the rich could afford his chic.

His world did change like he had wanted and the clear days in the sun finally ended up fuzzy.

I have a cry wolf taped shut in a shoe box under the fridge. It likes to be in a cooler environment so it can complain about it.

I often times wonder if I should throw it out, but the thought of separation gives me anxiety. It has me where it wants me.

Sometimes it screams and scares the neighbours. Other times, it sits in silence, unnoticed. I often times wonder if I should call for help when it gets angry, but it quickly calms itself into remission.

It's been a challenge living under the same roof together. I am not one for sudden loud noises; they make my heart skip an unhealthy number of beats. Not knowing when or why it might have an episode puts me on permanent emotional standby.

We've lived together for years. I don't remember my life without it, although on occasion some flashes of my past resurface at the most inconvenient times. I shut them out altogether. It can sense when I'm reminiscing, and I try not to draw unnecessary attention.

My friends keep asking if there is anything they can do to help, but that question really bores me. Courtesy mannerisms are pointless. One might as well keep to their own business instead of draining the little life I have left with such shit.

The box got broken into last night. The clues say my rat infestation might have finally got the best of us. My cables also took quite a hit, so watching television might require some additional effort. It sucks, too, because I was really getting into this show.

I now have a rat in a cage on my fridge, with a cry wolf in its belly.

I watch him standing there screwing it in with this look of complexity. I'm laying on my back in bed, my hair hanging off the side, soaking in the water I spilled on the floor while trying to cure my hangover.

The dog is asleep beside me, probably dreaming about last night and the champagne he licked off the floor after the countdown.

New Year's Eve has always been a complicated rollercoaster of emotions, mostly pertaining to the accomplishments the year helped me achieve.

This year however, felt like more of a collective feeling, as if the world stood still, taking in the last breath that 2020 had to offer amongst all the disasters it had already put us through. All waiting for the countdown to end, so we can begin into what some might see as a fresh start.

We are now in 2021. It feels like electing a new president that will either continue destroying its country, or slowly mend it again through drips and bandages. No one knows, and we all wait for the screw to either hold it all in or break.

I keep watching him work as my dog snores away the last drop of that 2020 champagne.

It was this time of year that the pot was boiling on my stove with a raspberry smell and a hint of chocolate. I wanted to believe it was done so I could taste it, but it seems a watched pot really never finishes. Neither did I that night.

It was a perfect. I got everything ready, I was prepared. An unfair life, but a fool consumed by obsession is just that, a fool. You stepped through my door like the perfect statue you were, an unfortunately emotionless specimen with perfect muscles. I felt lucky, a fox in her prime easily catching prey she can play with for a while. A fun thought, a sad reality.

I was barely able to serve you the drink I so carefully made. Your clothes were already being ripped to the floor with such an unfortunate desire. Two should have played your game that night.

Your lips were a stale, cracked imagination of the Sahara Desert, lonely, confused, and so tastelessly bare. My clothes still on while you stood there so vulnerably naked didn't give me the power I desired. It just made you look weak.

The man in my room I had wanted to fuck was now not intriguing enough to me to be fun. It was a strange realization that your beautifully carved body was never going to be enough to make a woman satisfied.

You tried. A kiss on the neck, a nibble on the ear. All the typical things one would do on a first date. Not quite my thing. Like the dripping water from a fountain I was not.

When you left, I sat waiting for a chance to shake the strangeness I felt when you touched me, a distanced feeling from a man too near for me to bare. Let me be clearer, I hated everything you were and all you continue to represent.

And yet I continue to masturbate to your memory.

I am terrified of dying. So much so, anything related to death puts me in a lump sum of legs and arms shoved in a corner facing just enough wall to feel safe. I hate it.

It all started when my aunt died in her sleep due to a brain aneurysm. Wrapping my head around the thought that you can kiss someone goodnight, never to wake up to them again is close to… "Um, no".

The fear is probably a useless one, especially because I can't control death. And yet, I find myself in tears picturing when death will come. We go through life thinking it's the enemy that ends all, takes away the you, leaves behind the remains you have no control of, and smirks at the hope that your family might have actually read the letter attached to your will and scattered you over Mount Kilimanjaro like you've always dreamed of. We reconcile with it through preparations: life insurances, wills, savings accounts, hoping to leave behind a safe haven for our loved ones.

Somewhere in this cluster of vast fear and precaution, I have forgotten I am currently very much alive - locked up in my house so that others can also have a fighting chance at life. There's a sense of unity with the world as I sit here trying to remember what my friends used to look like.

I think it must be a life lesson of some sort.

Even when I do get in touch with friends, I have a hard time catching them up. It's like a ping pong game of "How are yous?" and "What's news?", both sides feeling a lack of conversation that used to be so natural. How do you talk about the internal growth, the pain, the struggles, and the setbacks when they are all brand new to you? I sometimes don't even recognise myself through this new lens of isolation. It was easier when I could talk about my awful trips to London, or my first hangover at a gay bar where I met one of my best friends, or any story about something that actually happened.

I often think about how our generation will go down in history.

Our grandparents went to war, telling us stories of their battles. What will we tell our grandkids? That we complained about being stuck inside for a few months while the clubs shut down? That we laughed at people in power until they made us cry? That we took too long to fight for equality until one too many people died? We might just need to tell them that we were always a step behind, but always had the right intentions.

I am terrified of dying because I don't know how our story will be told.

I end up on this hill a lot, looking down at the people whose lives continue to pass by while mine runs still, a sad irony that is not lost on me. The houses look like a miniature architectural mockup; the people just working ants, busy doing their jobs.

Mary is probably still tending to her chocolate shop, working until those late hours of the night like she used to, so that when the morning comes her customers can buy her freshly made goodies. They really are something special.

John, her husband, is behind the counter counting the money they earned that day hoping it will be enough to pay back the unhappy customer that dropped the freshly baked chocolate cake Mary spent all day making.

Tina keeps singing at the bar across town knowing one day she will make it big. The crowd keeps throwing drinks at her but her commitment to her art is bigger than a few wet see-through T-shirts as her breasts illuminate the stage.

Katherine jogs every morning and swims in her private pool every night. She has never understood the struggles of life or that you need to work to attain materialistic things or experiences. Money has never been a problem for her. That is, what many would call, "pure fucking luck".

Timmy keeps disappearing for days and then appearing at the worst times. Being one of the only teenagers in town is hard for him, because he just doesn't quite fit in. The world is just too unfair for him right now and he has trouble handling it.

Everyone forgot about my death last week though. I was taking a stroll down to the corner store where Bob works, just to get a few snacks. I saw Jeffy stuck in a tree across the street and thought what a shame it must be to cry for help with no one listening. I thought the cat deserved a break, and since the local firefighters were busy saving Cindy's life across town from a burning building, I decided to cross the street. A poor decision on my part, especially given the fact I forgot the basic rule taught to us all as children: always look left first.

Poor Jeffy; I hope he made it down.

This is what the routine looks like: he goes to work for about two weeks, is gone for one, and then spends the next few days in the hospital. Not what one would call the best life. I would like to feel sorry for the guy, but he does it to himself which is the worst part. Why would you want to live a life like that?

Jack is one of the many people that fail at committing suicide. He isn't generally depressed either, but when a moment of true passion hits, and that passion mixes with that severe emptiness, he just has to go for the knife.

You'd think he'd learn by now that killing yourself just isn't that simple. It takes a lot to off yourself, and most people fail because they just don't do it well enough; and thank God for that. Hospitals get tired of those teenagers short of a few pills that decided their first breakup was just too much to continue living.

Not Jack though, he takes his tragedies to a whole other level. Jack likes to bleed publicly. All over the grocery stores, all over the parking lot, and once, all over a wedding dress. He wants people to watch, to pay attention, and ultimately, wants to live. This fascinating mental cycle of Jack's has him landing in the hospital monthly; the surgeon knows him by name.

One month however, Jack decided to stop. What's interesting about that is we all came to ask ourselves "What's wrong with Jack this month?" like it was somehow normal that cutting his wrists was the norm, and not doing so made him crazy.

The reason for this break was a girl; beautiful, tall, and blue eyed. He had fallen hard. She was European, with a heavy German accent and gorgeous blonde hair. On the outside, she was his perfection, a perfect piece for his puzzle mind.

One day however, Natasha did succeed where so many fail. She left without even a note to explain why. She was serious about it. She just wanted to be gone. Her attempt was successful because she chose a method that could never fail; she drove up a mountain and flew off the other side. Clean break.

Jack grieved for weeks. One month passed by, two months passed by, and after three years of not attempting anything, I just had to know.

"Hey Jack, why'd you stop?" I asked.

"Got bored." he said.

I had to double check that I had heard right. "You got bored?"

"Yeah."

I didn't know what to respond to that. His answer took me by surprise.
"Why do you ask?" he said.

"Honestly, because everyone in town is wondering; they just don't have the guts to ask." I said.

"That's the thing about people, they spend so much unnecessary time asking themselves questions that have no answer. What a waste of life." he said.

"So it really is that simple then, huh? You just got bored?" I said.

"Exactly."

To this day I still wonder how the answer could have been so simple. With so much heartache, I somehow wanted the answer to be deeper, more painful; for my entertainment, so that I could have had a story to tell everyone and be the center of attention. I wanted that high, the rush of knowing what others didn't, and being the first to find out.

I wonder if part of him knew that.

I'm obsessed with you. Wherever you go, whatever you do, I want you. I know your weaknesses, things that scare you, how to get under your skin. When I watch you undress in front of your window it feels like you want people to watch; or do you want me to watch? I don't like hearing about the ones that came before me and got a taste of you, but if I don't listen to what you say, how will I ever match them, be better than them, beat them at their game? You text me when you have hard times, I come pick you back up, and then you fuck them instead of me.

This new toy you take into your bed is scum, did you know that? A shit lawyer that puts good people behind bars just to make a little bit more money at the end of the day. Your taste in toys leaves something to be desired, darling.

I'm tired of sleeping in my car just to make sure you are alright. If you just chose me instead of them, things would be so much easier, relaxing, loving. We could be together, and I could keep you safe. Being in love with you is driving me insane. I know you find safety with me, company, because you know me. I'm familiar. Is that why you don't want me, because there just isn't enough mystery to keep you interested? How the fuck am I supposed to change that?

Morning comes and there goes the lawyer, walking out of your apartment without a care in world. Another day hard at work while you wash off your night endeavors under a cold shower with some morning whiskey. You are beautiful, perfect in fact, and I stand in front of your window picturing myself under that stream of water with you.

Starting with some light kisses on your neck and working my way down to your back, I spin you around and work my way back up to your collarbone. Slowly taking off your clothes I make sure the bathroom steams up just right, ditching that cold shower you think you want. I would make you mine better than others ever have, I can promise you that.

You were supposed to warn me before you cut so deep into my soul, love. I wasn't prepared, and I don't appreciate that. Maybe when they come looking for us, they will understand how unfair you've been. I don't expect you to understand me. I don't expect you to want to. I don't love her; you should know that. She is a replacement for the pain you caused. For the emptiness I feel because you never saw me, you never wanted me, you just never fucking cared. So, when you find us, think of me for one of your shitty selfish seconds, because I know I would have been the best you've ever had.

How much do you think that this house is worth? Just look at these doors, they must cost thousands. My truck is outside in the sun, and I know once I come back those seats are going to be boiling. I hate my job; I have no idea how I ended up here. This box is extremely heavy, but I am hesitating to put it down for some reason. The house just feels odd to me, and there's no one home. What if someone steals this, then it's going to be my fault for not being careful enough. I should probably check around the house to see if there might be another spot I can put this.

All of the doors seem closed and I am still carrying this heavy thing. What's in here anyway? I need to put this down for a second, my hands are about to give in. I know this house, I deliver their mail every day and yet somehow today it just feels oddly quiet. Someone is always home, and most of the time what I assume are the husband and wife argue loudly. It's always about really boring stuff, like where the silverware goes, and how he needs to rinse the dishes before her puts them in the dishwasher. It's really much too quiet today.

My car is heating up and I left my door open which is going to be an extra blow. I hate my work in the summer, especially because I always have to have my windows down so it never cools off. I feel like I have been standing here awkwardly for the last ten minutes. Why can't I just leave? I think I should open the front door. Well, it's unlocked. Oh no, what do I do now? Now I definitely can't leave, they forgot to lock their door. I need to stay here to guard the house.

It's getting really hot out here. It feels really cool in there. I shouldn't go in though, that would be an invasion of privacy. Or would it be, if I am only doing it for selfless reasons? I am after all, just protecting them. Alright, I'm going in, but I am just going to sit on the couch until I feel like it is safe to leave.

Oh no, I must have dozed off. What's the time? Do I hear them coming? I need to get out of here fast.

"Honey, why is the mailman's car here?" asks the wife.

"Not sure, it seems to still be running. How strange."

"Do you see him anywhere?"

"I don't think so. Wasn't Annie's package supposed to arrive today?" he says.

"That's what she told me."

I hear them approaching the house. Hiding in the bathroom was not the most clever idea. I should have just unlocked one of the other eight doors in the house and ran. I am so stupid.

"Did you forget to lock the door?" she says.

"That's the third time that happened to me. I'm sorry honey, maybe it's time I finally see that doctor you recommended."

They are inside the house now. I can't go anywhere, I'm officially stuck here.

"Honey, is this the package?" she asks.

"How on earth did this get inside?" he asks.

"Maybe it came this morning and you forgot about it? It wouldn't be the first time, you know. We really should get you checked." she says.

I need to get out of here before they realize I'm here.

"I will be right back to help with those groceries, just going to the bathroom." she says.

Well, now I'm screwed.

I hide into their bathroom closet. I can barely fit in here. What's that smell? Please let this be over soon, I can't breathe in here. I can hear her coming into the bathroom, door is opening and closing, the sink turns on, and the shower? Is she taking a shower? What the fuck is happening, I can't stay here for…

"So, do you want to come out or should I make you come out?"

Fuck. Who is she talking to? Is she on the phone?

"I won't ask twice."

I need to stay perfectly still. Don't breathe. Don't move.

She opens the closet.

I've been kicking this stupid pebble for over 5 minutes, and I probably moved an inch. School's out and I need to be walking home to meet my parents for lunch, but I just can't seem to get myself moving. They just haven't been my safe space lately, and I feel like I'm going through a lot of shit. I'm often misunderstood and when I try to be polite and nice, I am just seen as selfish. Such is a day in the life of a teenager.

My days are overwhelmed by thoughts of failure. I'm not doing enough at home, my grades aren't what my parents want them to be, I don't have any raw talents for art or music, and most of all, I can't seem to get myself motivated enough to accomplish much. Not the best.

I have a boyfriend who is into playing video games, so when we aren't in school I don't really see him much. I tried to get into the world of consoles and controllers, but it really doesn't interest me. So aside from making out in the hallway and pissing off our teachers, there is not much there in the love department of moi.

My sense of style is very somber. Mostly dark greys and blacks. I don't like to showcase myself in front of people or give them any reason to judge me; I do that enough myself. Honesty is something I value above all else, so if I catch you in lie you have probably lost my trust forever. This little quirk of mine burned itself into my brain after I walked in on my mother having sex with a man that was not my father when I was 7. Not a memory I had hoped would stick around, but it has and now I live with it by not being a lying whore.

"Hey sweetie, how was school?" asks my mom.

Yay, I made it home just in time for lunch. I wonder what's on today's menu from all the three meals we ever eat.

"Your dad can't make it today. He is stuck at work."

Of course he is. Ever since he fired poor Rhonda, his secretary of fifteen years, and got a newer, much younger model, dad has been missing family lunches often. Mom knows, but she is too busy downing bottles of red Merlot to care. She can't really be the one to say anything, she started it.

"What's for lunch, mom?" I ask.

"I thought we could just order in today. It's that kind of a day."

Beats her cooking by a long shot, so I eagerly oblige with that request. Pizza sounds nice right about now. Dad won't be home for hours since he is too busy screwing Amanda on the front desk, and mom's two bottles are starting to show, so she'll be out cold here shortly.

When the curtains close behind our white picket fence the demons really do come out. Picture perfect family on the outside, broken as shit on the inside. A story that will never be told. What the heck, I'm 16 now, maybe a glass of red for me as well?

"What do you say mom? Can I join you with a glass of wine?"

"Sure thing sweetie."

My future is bright.

I sing my heart out to kids at birthday parties, at home, while they drive in cars, anywhere! It's my job if we want to be more specific. The songs most requested are "Twinkle Twinkle Little Star", "The Itsy Bitsy Spider", and "The Happy Song". If you woke me up at 3am, I could sing those to you in reverse.

I've been doing this for 8 years now, and I don't plan on stopping. My voice is the one thing that never runs out, my most reliable instrument.

Today however, I lost my voice. Gone. Kaput. Nothing there. My most important performance of the year is in 4 hours, and I have nothing to offer but a creak.

I tried everything. Hot water, lemon, honey, steam, rest. Nothing.

Two hours before the show and I can't speak, let alone sing.

I showed up anyway.

Walked out on that stage with 200 kids staring at me like I was their whole world.

Opened my mouth.

And they sang. Every single word, every note, every silly sound effect. They knew every song better than I did.

I stood there mouthing the words as 200 children performed for me.

Turns out I wasn't the instrument. I was just the reason they found their voice.

My grandmother collected spoons. Not silver ones, not antique ones, not ones with any real value to speak of. She collected the cheap souvenir kind from every place she'd ever been. Plastic handles, painted flags, tiny engraved city names that were already fading by the time she hung them.

When she died, we spent three days deciding what to do with the collection.

Nobody wanted the spoons.

Everybody wanted to talk about the spoons.

My uncle remembered the one from Niagara Falls and the road trip they took when he was nine. My mother cried over the Dublin spoon, the one trip grandma took without the family, alone at sixty-two, just to see where her own grandmother came from.

There was one from a town none of us recognized. Small place. No one knew when she went or who she went with.

We never found out.

In the end we divided them up. I took six. I don't collect spoons, I don't have a place to hang them, and I have moved four times since.

They come with me anyway.

Some things you keep not because they're valuable, but because throwing them away would mean admitting the person is really gone.

The last text I sent her was about a parking ticket.

I was annoyed about it. Fourteen dollars. I sent her a photo of the ticket and three angry emojis and she sent back a laughing face and told me to appeal it, that I always won when I appealed.

She was right. I always won.

That was a Thursday. She was gone by Sunday.

For a long time after, I couldn't stop thinking about the parking ticket. That fourteen dollars, those three emojis. Out of everything I could have said in what turned out to be the last conversation we would ever have, that's what I chose.

I've appealed every parking ticket since. I win most of them.

I don't know why I keep doing it. She's not here to tell me she told me so. There's no one waiting for the update.

I send the result to her number anyway. Still not disconnected.

Somewhere in my phone, she has an unread string of small victories she'll never see.

I think that's the closest thing I have left to talking to her.

He proposed on a Tuesday. Not a special Tuesday, just a Tuesday in the middle of a grocery run. They were standing in the cereal aisle and he had a box of the wrong kind in his hand and she was about to correct him when he said it.

Just like that. No ring, no plan, no bended knee. Just him, holding the wrong cereal, looking at her like she was the only right thing in the room.

She said yes before she meant to. Or maybe she meant to and didn't know it yet.

They finished the shopping. They got home, they put everything away. They ate dinner. She kept looking at him over the table like she was waiting for him to admit he was joking.

He wasn't joking.

They went to bed and she lay there in the dark thinking about how she had always imagined the moment would feel enormous, cinematic, a thing she would describe to her daughters someday with her hands moving and her voice going soft.

Instead it felt like exhaling.

Like a window finally opening in a room she hadn't realised was stuffy.

In the morning he made coffee and handed her a mug and their hands touched the same way they always did, and she thought yes, that's it, that's the thing, that ordinary Tuesday touch.

She still has the cereal box. Wrong kind. Kept it anyway.

Some proposals don't need a ring. They just need the right person holding the wrong cereal.

The dog knew before any of us did.

Three days before my father's diagnosis, the dog stopped sleeping at the foot of the bed and started sleeping pressed against his side. Wouldn't leave the room. Followed him to the bathroom, to the kitchen, back again. Sat with his head on my father's knee every evening like he was keeping vigil.

My father thought it was funny. "He thinks I'm dying," he said, laughing.

Nobody laughed with him.

The vet said dogs can smell certain changes in body chemistry. Shifts in hormones, cellular activity, things we don't have instruments sensitive enough to catch. They just know. They've always known.

My father got through it. Surgery, then recovery, then the slow climb back.

The dog went back to sleeping at the foot of the bed.

Sometimes I think about what it means to love something without the ability to explain what's wrong. To just sit beside it, stay close, press yourself against the warmth of it because you can feel something shifting and you have no language for it except presence.

The dog was onto something.

We all should love like that.

My neighbor has been watering the same dead plant for six months.

I noticed it in October, the leaves brown and curled, the soil cracked in spite of the water she keeps pouring into it every morning at seven-fifteen. I can see her from my kitchen window, still in her robe, watering can in hand, tilting it carefully over something that stopped being alive a long time ago.

I almost knocked on her door once. I had a whole sentence rehearsed.

I didn't knock.

I watched her all winter. She never missed a morning. Seven-fifteen, robe, watering can.

In March, something happened.

I don't know the science of it. I don't know if a seed was dormant or if it was a different plant entirely and I just hadn't been paying close enough attention.

But there was green.

Actual, undeniable green.

She didn't celebrate. She just kept watering, same as always.

I think she always knew. I think she just had more patience than me.

I met a man on a plane once who told me he had never once in his life sent a text message he regretted.

I didn't believe him.

He wasn't boasting, he was just stating a fact the way you'd say you've never broken a bone or never learned to swim. Calm, a little puzzled that it needed saying.

I asked him how.

He said he wrote everything twice. Once for himself, to get it out, to feel it. Then again for the person he was sending it to. The first draft he always deleted. The second one he sent.

He'd been doing it since he got his first phone. Almost forty years.

I asked him if he ever missed sending the first draft.

He thought about it for a long time. We were somewhere over the Atlantic.

"Sometimes," he said. "But you can't take things back. And I'd rather be understood than right."

We landed. He put on his jacket, wished me safe travels, and walked off into arrivals.

I never got his name.

I think about him every time I type something angry and almost send it.

I don't always write it twice.

But I think about him. And most of the time, that's enough.

My mother kept a drawer of things that had no place else to go.

Batteries that might still work. A key to something no one remembered locking. Rubber bands, takeaway menus for places that had closed, a birthday candle that had been blown out and saved, three foreign coins, a magnet in the shape of a fish, instructions for an appliance she no longer owned.

She called it the useful drawer.

Nothing in it was ever useful.

When she moved, we spent an afternoon going through it together. She couldn't throw most of it away. "That key might still open something," she said. "You never know."

I kept the fish magnet. Don't know why.

I have my own drawer now. A key I don't recognize. An instruction manual. A birthday candle. Some coins from a trip I took years ago.

I call it the junk drawer.

But sometimes I open it and I feel something I don't have a name for, something between comfort and longing.

I think maybe I finally understand the useful drawer.

It was never about the things.

It was about holding onto the possibility that something might still matter.

She left every party early.

Not rudely, she was always gracious about it, touched arms, said goodbyes, thanked the host twice. But she always left before the night peaked, before the second wind, before the dancing started or the serious conversations broke open.

Everyone assumed she had somewhere to be. A child at home, an early morning, a responsible life requiring attendance.

She had none of those things.

What she had was this: she liked the walk home. That specific walk, in that specific in-between hour when the night was still happening somewhere behind her and the quiet of the street felt like a secret she was keeping. The twenty minutes between being among people and being home. The cool air and the sound of her own footsteps.

She had discovered, by accident, that this was her favourite part of any evening.

Not the party. The walk away from it.

Not the conversation, but the silence after.

Not the people, but the feeling of having been with them, still warm on her skin, already becoming memory.

She never explained this to anyone.

She suspected no one would understand why you'd leave a good thing early just to savour the missing of it.

But she also suspected, sometimes, that everyone understood exactly what she meant, and that was why no one ever asked her to stay.

I used to write letters to people I'd lost arguments with.

Not to send. Never to send. Just to write. I'd sit down with a pen and say every sharp thing I hadn't managed in the moment, make all the points I'd only thought of on the drive home, land every comeback that came three hours too late.

I was very good at it.

The letters felt satisfying for about twenty minutes. Then they just felt embarrassing, so I'd burn them or tear them up or bury them in the recycling under other things.

At some point I stopped.

I'm not sure when or why exactly. I just noticed one day that I hadn't written one in years.

I think what changed is that I stopped needing to win as much. Not because I became patient or enlightened. More because I started to notice that the arguments I lost were usually the ones where the other person was right, and I was just too embarrassed to say so at the time.

The letters were never really about winning.

They were about not knowing how to say I'm sorry.

I'm still not great at saying it out loud.

But at least I'm not burning paper anymore.

There's a man who sits outside the coffee shop on the corner every morning at half past seven. Same chair, same paper cup, same coat regardless of season. He doesn't read, doesn't look at a phone. He just sits and watches the street.

I've been walking past him for three years.

For a long time I assumed he was waiting for something. Waiting for someone. A person who was running late, a bus he kept missing, some resolution that hadn't arrived yet.

Last winter I stopped and asked him what he was doing.

He looked at me like I'd asked a very strange question.

"Watching," he said.

I asked him what he was watching for.

"Nothing in particular," he said. "Just watching."

He seemed slightly sorry for me, in a gentle way.

I bought my coffee and kept walking and thought about it all day.

I live my entire life waiting for the next thing. The meeting, the weekend, the resolution. Always arriving somewhere in my head before my body gets there.

He just sits. Present. Watching nothing in particular.

I wonder who's getting more out of mornings.

I found a journal in a second-hand bookshop. Not a blank one, a used one, already written in.

Thirty-seven pages of someone's year. The handwriting was small and careful, the kind that's been practiced. The entries were ordinary, grocery lists that bled into feelings, arguments summarized then crossed out, a handful of evenings that clearly meant something to whoever was writing, weather observations, a recurring name that stopped appearing around page twenty and was never explained.

I bought it.

I've thought about that decision many times since. Whether it was right to buy someone's private record of a year. Whether the person who sold it wanted someone to find it, or whether they just needed it gone.

I read it once, slowly. Then I put it away.

I know small things now about a stranger. What they ate on certain evenings. A fear they had about their mother. The name that stopped appearing.

I've never told anyone about the journal.

It sits in my own bookshelf now, between other books, spine out, indistinguishable.

Sometimes I wonder if they're out there. If they ever think about that year. If they'd want to know someone found it.

I think I'd want to know.

I think.

She asked me once what I thought happened after.

We were sitting on the back step, late, the kind of late where the dark feels like a presence and you say things you wouldn't say in the day.

I said I didn't know. Which was true.

She said she hoped it was like being in a warm room full of everyone you'd ever loved, all of them at different ages, everyone fine, no one in pain.

I said that sounded nice.

She said she knew it was probably not how it worked. But she said hoping costs nothing and fear costs everything, so she'd decided a long time ago to just pick the version she liked and live with that.

I thought about that for a long time after. The deliberateness of it. Choosing what to believe not because it was proven but because it was liveable.

She's been gone four years now.

I don't know what happens after. I still don't.

But I've started hoping for the warm room.

It costs nothing.

And she'd be there.

The man in the apartment above me plays the same song every Sunday morning.

I don't know what the song is. I've looked it up by humming it into my phone and the app can never find it. I've Googled fragments of the melody the way you'd describe a dream: rising, then dropping, then three quick notes, then slow. Nothing.

I've lived below him for four years.

In that time I've heard the song maybe two hundred times. I know it better than most songs I've deliberately learned. I could hum it to you right now and you would either recognize it immediately or you wouldn't and we'd both be stuck.

I don't know his name. I've seen him maybe six times. Grey hair, quiet, nods in the hallway. Looks like someone who has made peace with most things.

Some Sundays the song is louder, some Sundays barely there. Once it played twice in a row. Once it didn't play at all and I sat in my kitchen for an hour feeling like something was wrong with the day.

I'm scared of the morning when it stops.

I've never told him it exists as a thing for me.

I wonder if he knows. I wonder if the song is for him or for someone else.

I wonder if someone somewhere misses hearing it.

My father taught me to drive in an empty car park on a Sunday morning.

He wasn't a patient man in general. He had opinions about the right way to do things and a low tolerance for the wrong way. But in that car park, for those six Sundays, he was someone I didn't entirely recognize.

He talked me through everything twice. He didn't raise his voice when I mounted the curb. When I stalled four times in a row on what should have been a simple turn, he said, simply, "again," and waited.

On the last Sunday, I got it. Smoothly, perfectly, in a way that surprised both of us. I felt the car respond the right way and I looked at him and he was grinning, the unselfconscious kind, the kind I'd seen maybe three times in my life.

"There it is," he said.

I don't think he was talking only about the driving.

He died six years later. There are so many conversations I didn't have with him, so many questions I assumed we had more time for.

But I have those Sundays.

I have the way he said "again" without making it feel like a failure.

I have the grin.

Sometimes when I'm driving, smooth and easy, I think: there it is.

And I mean it the way he did.

When I was eight, I convinced myself the dark had a smell.

Not a scary smell. Just a smell that wasn't there in the day. Like something settling, something exhaling. Cold and a little like old paper and something else I could never name.

I mentioned it once at dinner and my sister told me I was weird and my parents changed the subject, so I never brought it up again.

But I kept noticing it. Every night when the light went out. That particular smell that was only there when I couldn't see.

I'm thirty-four now.

I still notice it.

I looked it up once. There is apparently some science to it: the brain, deprived of visual input, amplifies other senses. You might smell things in the dark that were there all along, just below the threshold of your attention.

I liked that explanation less than my childhood one.

I preferred the idea that the dark had something of its own to offer. Its own atmosphere. Its own particular presence.

Something settling. Something exhaling.

Like the world breathing out after a long day of being looked at.

I've been mispronouncing a word for thirty years.

I only found out last Tuesday.

A colleague said it correctly in a meeting and I thought she'd made a mistake and then I looked it up under the table and discovered that I had been wrong every single time, in every conversation, in every context, for three decades.

The strange thing is I don't know how I never got corrected.

Either no one noticed, or they noticed and said nothing, or they noticed and forgot immediately because it's not the kind of thing that tends to matter.

For a day or two I felt a specific kind of embarrassment about it. The retroactive kind, where you go back and replay moments and cringe at something that at the time felt fine.

Then I thought about all the words I probably still have wrong. The ones no one's corrected yet. The things I say with complete confidence that are, quietly, slightly off.

And I found that oddly comforting.

There is so much I don't know about the ways I'm wrong.

Which means there is so much left to find out.

Tuesday was a good day, in the end.

I said the word correctly on the way home. Quietly. To myself. Just to hear it.

I had a friend who remembered the exact outfit she was wearing for almost every significant moment of her life.

Not in a vain way. Just in the way that some people remember by smell or by sound, she remembered by clothing. The dress she wore the day her parents told her they were separating. The coat she had on when she got the call about the job. Jeans and a green shirt, her first heartbreak. A yellow sundress, the best summer of her life.

She said it wasn't something she chose to do. The memory just came attached to the fabric.

I found it strange at first. Then I found it beautiful. She had an entire archive of her life organized by what she'd been wearing, which meant every piece of clothing in her wardrobe was also a place.

She could travel by opening her closet.

I asked her once if she ever got rid of anything.

She said yes, sometimes. When you want to leave a memory behind, she said, you give away what you were wearing.

I've been thinking about that differently ever since.

I've been thinking about what's hanging in my own wardrobe.

What I'm keeping.

What I'm still not ready to let go of.

I make lists of things I've never done and probably never will.

Not sad ones. Neutral ones. Things I simply ran out of road for, or never had the right circumstances, or chose not to, or kept meaning to and then time just arranged itself otherwise.

Learn to sail. Spend a month in a country where I don't speak the language. Raise chickens. Get really good at chess. Own a library, an actual one, with a ladder on wheels. Go somewhere so remote there's no signal.

I don't feel the list as loss. I feel it more as proof that I had more life than I could fit.

That I was interested in more things than I had time for.

That I had enough curiosity to fill several lives and only got to use one.

I've heard people talk about bucket lists like they're debts to settle before you go.

Mine doesn't feel like that.

Mine feels like evidence.

Evidence that the world was interesting.

Evidence that I noticed.

Evidence that there was always something else I could have loved, if given the chance.

I think that's enough.

I think that might be everything.

I went to a funeral once for someone I barely knew.

Not by accident. I chose to go. She was the mother of someone I'd met twice, maybe three times, a woman whose name I'd heard in passing, whose face I recognized from a photo on someone else's phone.

I went because the person who loved her asked me to come, quietly, in a way that wasn't quite asking, and I understood that the room needed to be fuller than it was going to be.

I sat in the back.

The eulogies were specific in the way the best ones always are. Not about what a good person she was in abstract, but about the way she folded napkins, the particular stubbornness she had about one brand of tea, the noise she made when she was pretending not to find something funny.

I left knowing more about her than I did when I arrived.

I've thought about her since. This woman I never met. Her napkins and her tea and that particular suppressed laugh.

I think that's the point of a funeral, actually. Not to say goodbye, but to give strangers something to carry.

So the person doesn't just live in the people who knew them.

They live a little in everyone who sat in the room.

I carried her out of there.

I still have her.

There's a photograph of my parents before I existed.

They're young in it, younger than I am now, which is still strange to me. My mother is laughing at something outside the frame. My father has his hand on her shoulder but he's looking at the camera, serious in the way young men sometimes are in photographs because they think seriousness reads as dignity.

Neither of them knows yet that I'm coming.

I love that photograph for reasons I can't fully explain. Something about seeing them as people who had a whole life before they had to be parents. Before they had to be anything to me at all.

They were just two people at a party. One of them laughing. One of them trying to look serious.

Someone thought to take the picture. Someone thought this moment mattered enough to keep.

I think about that a lot. The moments that were kept and the moments that weren't. All the versions of them I'll never see.

The people they were before I made them parents.

The love that existed before it had to make room for me.

I hope it was as light as it looks in that photo.

I hope they got more evenings like that one.

My grandfather used to say there are two kinds of silence.

The kind that waits for something to fill it, and the kind that's already full.

I didn't understand that for a long time. Silence was silence. Absence of noise. I didn't see how it could be holding anything.

Then one evening I was sitting with someone I loved, and we weren't talking, and I noticed that the quiet between us felt like something. Not empty. Not waiting. Just there, settled, the way a room feels after a fire has been lit in it.

I thought: this is the kind that's already full.

I understand now that there's a whole spectrum. The silence at a dinner table when something has gone wrong. The silence after an apology that hasn't been accepted. The silence of a room when someone who used to be in it isn't anymore.

And then the other kind. The one my grandfather was talking about.

The silence between two people who have nothing to prove to each other.

I've spent a lot of my life trying to fill silences that were already full.

I'm getting better at recognizing the difference.

Slowly.

I keep a running list of things I was wrong about.

Not mistakes I made, specifically. More like convictions I held that turned out to be the wrong shape for the world.

I was wrong that certain people were irreplaceable. Some of them became replaceable so quickly it frightened me.

I was wrong that I couldn't live without certain things. I lived without them.

I was wrong about what I would find hard, and wrong about what would turn out to be easy.

I was wrong that time heals. Time doesn't heal anything. You heal, slowly, using time as raw material, and even then the scar tissue is different from the original.

I was wrong about the kind of person I thought I was.

That one I'm still working on. The list keeps growing.

Every time I add something to it I feel, paradoxically, a little lighter. Like the list is a thing that can hold the weight so I don't have to.

I'm wrong about something right now. I just don't know what yet.

I think that's fine.

I think that's human.

The summer I was twelve, I had a best friend who moved away in August.

We wrote letters for the first year. Real ones, on paper, with stamps. We had things to say and we said them carefully in the way you do when you know the person won't get it for a week and you want it to still make sense when they do.

The second year the letters got shorter. Then they turned into the early internet, quick messages with no punctuation, the kind that felt like talking but weren't quite.

By the third year we had nothing left to say that wasn't about the lives we were living without each other, and those lives didn't overlap anymore.

I've thought about her often over the years. Not with grief, exactly. More with a kind of tenderness for the friendship and for the people we were inside it.

I saw her name somewhere recently. She's married. Two kids. Lives somewhere I've never been.

I didn't reach out.

Some friendships don't need an ending or a revival. They just need to have existed.

The letters were real.

The summer was real.

That's enough.

That's everything.

I started this because I needed somewhere to put things.

Not big things. Not the dramatic moments that announce themselves and demand to be processed. The other things. The small, persistent things that don't have a category. The observation you make on the way to work that doesn't fit into a conversation. The feeling that arrives on a Sunday afternoon with no name. The memory that surfaces in the shower and is gone before you can look at it directly.

I didn't know what I was doing when I started. I'm still not sure I do.

I just know that writing it down did something to it. Changed its shape. Made it smaller and more real at the same time.

So I kept going.

If you've read this far, you've been holding my small things for a while now.

Thank you for that.

I hope somewhere in here you found one of your own.

Help yourself to a cup of something warm.

Stay as long as you like.
